page_hint: Ch 15, 'Two Mechanisms, Read as Mechanisms' → 'Speculative decoding' paragraph; and the Optimization Decision Map row 'high TPOT/ITL + HBM bandwidth saturated'
quoted_clause: quantization, batching up, speculative decoding, smaller active params, more bandwidth
observed: The chapter never states the condition under which speculative decoding actually reduces weight-stream traffic, and the decision map places it in precisely the regime where it does not help. Decode at batch B streams the full weight set once per step, so bytes/token = W/B. Speculative decoding with acceptance length k streams the weights once per k+1 tokens, so bytes/token = W/(k+1). The traffic saving is positive only when k+1 > B. At the chapter's own batch-32 test point (§4) with a typical k of 4, speculative decoding reduces bytes/token by zero while adding draft-model cost and verification overhead. This also puts the map in direct tension with §6, which recommends continuous batching (large B) as the primary decode lever.
correction: Add the batch condition to the mechanism paragraph: 'The saving exists only while the decode batch is smaller than the expected acceptance length k+1: at batch B the weights are already streamed once per step for B sequences (W/B bytes per token), so speculative decoding can only help when k+1 > B. At large batch, where the chapter's own continuous-batching recommendation puts the system, speculative decoding reduces weight traffic by nothing and adds draft cost.' Add 'current decode batch size vs expected acceptance length' to the map's evidence column and annotate the row accordingly.
evidence: W = 140 GB (FP16 70B). Batch-32 decode: 140/32 = 4.4 GB/token. Speculative with k=4: 140/5 = 28 GB/token — worse than batch-32 decode. Batch-1 decode: 140 GB/token vs 28 GB/token — a 5× saving. The saving therefore exists only in the low-batch regime, which is the opposite of the 'HBM bandwidth saturated' symptom the map attaches it to.

page_hint: Ch 17, counter-scenario A
quoted_clause: each generated token re-reads the full ~14 GB of weights, so the per-host decode token rate is capped by HBM bandwidth ÷ weight size
observed: This treats a batched decode step as if it re-read the full weight set once per generated token per request. In batched decode, the weights are read once per decode step and reused across all sequences in the batch. The per-host token rate is therefore approximately batch_size × HBM_bandwidth / weight_bytes, subject to compute and KV limits, not HBM_bandwidth / weight_bytes.
correction: Rewrite counter-scenario A in terms of decode steps and batch size: per-step weight traffic is ~14 GB, per-step token output is B, so token rate ≈ B × HBM_BW / weight_bytes, capped by compute and KV. Then show the actual binding constraint at the stated 200 rps × 100 output tokens, including the batch size needed and the KV/compute limits. Do not claim that HBM_BW / weight_bytes alone caps per-host token rate.
evidence: For a 7B FP16 model, weights ≈ 14 GB. On an H100 with ~3.35 TB/s HBM, a batch-1 decode step is bounded by 14 GB / 3.35 TB/s ≈ 4.18 ms, i.e. ~239 tokens/s for one sequence. At batch 100, the same weight read produces up to ~23,900 tokens/s before compute/KV limits. The chunk's formula gives only ~239 tokens/s and then concludes that 200 rps × 100 output tokens 'dwarfs' one host's bandwidth. That conclusion depends on ignoring batching, which the book elsewhere treats as central.

page_hint: Ch 17 §17.6 'Multi-region active-active availability is NOT priced in this chapter's arithmetic'
quoted_clause: every host count here — and the N−1 failover/redundancy model above — is a **single-region, N−1-only** number (≈21 peak / 31 working / 32 with N−1 — the KV screen under case (i); 22 peak / 33 working / 34 with N−1 under the **full-square case (ii) prefill compute screen**)
observed: The KV-residency screen is labelled with a prefill FLOP-counting case label. '(i)/(ii)/(iii)' are the prefill compute screen's FLOP-counting cases (defined in the Table 17-2 note: '19 hosts under case (i) (linear-only), 21 under case (iii) (causal-triangle), 22 under case (ii) (full-square conservative)'). The KV screen is not 'under case (i)'. Notably, case (iii) yields exactly 21 / 31 / 32, the same triple as the KV screen, which suggests '(i)' is a slip for '(iii)' - but as printed, the sentence attaches a prefill-case label to a KV screen, and the reader cannot tell which screen the 21/31/32 belongs to.
correction: Rename the prefill cases (for example 'prefill case P1/P2/P3' or 'linear-only / causal-triangle / full-square') so they cannot collide with the KV screen, and label the 21/31/32 triple explicitly as the KV-residency screen at T=0 FP16. If the intent was to note that the KV screen coincides with case (iii), say that.
evidence: Table 17-2 note: case (i) = 19 peak / 28 working / 29 with N-1; case (iii) = 21 peak / 31 working / 32 with N-1; case (ii) = 22 peak / 33 working / 34 with N-1. The KV screen at T=0 FP16 = 21 peak / 31 working / 32 with N-1.

page_hint: Ch 17, Table 17-2 closing note, final sentence
quoted_clause: Every one of 29/32/34/82/205/410 (no-reuse FP8 in the agentic columns) is an **illustrative planning screen under its stated FLOP-counting case and the 35% MFU assumption, not measured SLO-goodput.**
observed: The parenthetical mislabels the numbers it qualifies. 82/205/410 are the T=3 FP16 no-reuse row of Table 17-2 (C = 13, 8.645), not FP8 (the FP8 no-reuse row is 40/99/198). The sentence also attributes 'its stated FLOP-counting case and the 35% MFU assumption' to a list that mixes prefill-compute-screen numbers (29/32/34) with KV-residency-screen numbers (82/205/410), which are derived from no FLOP count and no MFU assumption at all. A reader who takes the sentence at face value will believe the agentic host counts are prefill-compute screens.

evidence: Table 17-2 rows: 'N @ T=3, FP16 no-reuse (C=13; 8.645)' = 82 / 205 / 410; 'N @ T=3, FP8 no-reuse (C=27; 17.955)' = 40 / 99 / 198. The 29/32/34 values are the prefill screens from the preceding sentence.

page_hint: Ch 17 §17.5 Common Mistakes #5
quoted_clause: GPU inference time is not constant; under sustained high load, kernel‑mode preemption, memory fragmentation, and concurrent kernel launches can increase per‑token latency by 20–50%. The linear model t = t_inference + t_tool is a lower bound; the architect should add a 20% safety margin.
observed: Two problems. (1) The 20-50% degradation range is an unsourced quantitative claim about a specific set of mechanisms, presented in the same register as the book's measured or derived numbers; it carries no evidence label and no source. (2) The prescribed remedy is inconsistent with the stated range: if per-token latency can rise 20-50%, a 20% safety margin covers only the bottom of the range and leaves the architect exposed at the top. 'kernel-mode preemption' is also ambiguous - it reads as OS kernel mode rather than GPU kernel time-slicing between concurrently resident kernels.
correction: Either source the 20-50% range (a measured or published result with its workload and hardware stated) and label it accordingly, or reframe it as an [ASSUMPTION] with the mechanism named. Then make the margin consistent with the range (e.g. 'size the margin against the upper end of the range, or measure the degradation on the target deployment') and rename 'kernel-mode preemption' to 'kernel time-slicing between concurrent GPU kernels'.
evidence: The book's own evidence-label vocabulary (Ch 4 / Appendix A) includes [ILLUSTRATIVE], [ASSUMPTION] and [HYPOTHESIS]; this range carries none. The margin (20%) is at the minimum of the stated range (20-50%).

page_hint: Ch 17 §17.6 'Load-balancer selection and configuration'
quoted_clause: Hardware L7 switches offer better ρ (≈0.98) but less fine‑grained traffic‑shaping; software LBs offer ρ ≈ 0.95 but can implement consistent hashing for session affinity. The architect should match the LB capability to the session model: sticky sessions → any LB; stateless → software LB with consistent hashing.
observed: The guidance is inverted. Consistent hashing is a session-affinity mechanism: it deliberately pins a key to a host. A stateless routing policy (any host may serve any request) wants least-connections or power-of-two-choices, not consistent hashing, which would reintroduce the affinity the policy is trying to avoid. The second clause also contradicts the first: if software LBs are the ones that 'can implement consistent hashing for session affinity', then 'sticky sessions -> any LB' is not true, and the hardware/software distinction the paragraph sets up is not the one that matters. The paragraph's real decision variable is whether the LB supports affinity at all, not whether it is hardware or software.
correction: Restate the decision as: (a) if the session model requires affinity, the LB must support it (consistent hashing or cookie/session pinning) - note that hardware L7 support varies by platform and must be verified; (b) if the session model is stateless, use least-connections or power-of-two-choices so that load follows capacity, and do not use consistent hashing. Keep the rho values as the cost of each choice, and note that the rho difference (0.98 vs 0.95) changes the host count by roughly 3% at the canonical fleet size.
evidence: The paragraph's own premises: hardware L7 = better rho, less shaping; software = lower rho, consistent hashing. The recommendation maps sticky sessions to 'any LB' and stateless to 'consistent hashing', which inverts both premises.

page_hint: Ch 18 §18.8 mini-case scope note
quoted_clause: *(Scope note: these tier per-token rates are illustrative scenario values that **differ from the §18.3.2 per-1M ledger** — they are not the ledger's $1.25 (8-bit) / $2.50 (FP16) / $0.15 (4-bit) per-1M rates converted, and the 4-bit tier's ~600 ms latency differs from the ledger's 800 ms. They are on a per-token basis, distinct from — and not directly comparable to — the per-1M-token ledger; the mini-case uses them to demonstrate the routing economics, and a real deployment would price from the §18.3.2 per-1M basis.)*
observed: The stated reason for the discrepancy is wrong, and the magnitude of the discrepancy is never disclosed. Per-token and per-1M rates are the same quantity in different units, so 'on a per-token basis, distinct from ... the per-1M-token ledger' is not a basis difference at all. Converted, the mini-case's rates are $200/1M (4-bit), $1,500/1M (8-bit) and $3,000/1M (FP16) against the ledger's $0.15, $1.25 and $2.50 - i.e. 1,333x, 1,200x and 1,200x higher. A reader who notices the gap is told the two are 'not directly comparable' without being told that they differ by three orders of magnitude or why.
correction: Rewrite the scope note to state the real reason: the mini-case prices a ~20 requests/hour pilot in which a dedicated host's cost is amortized over a negligible token volume, so its per-token rates are roughly three orders of magnitude above the fleet-scale ledger; the mini-case's absolute dollars are therefore not comparable to §18.3.3's, and only its internal ratios are meaningful. Alternatively, derive the mini-case's rates from the ledger so the two sections agree.

page_hint: Ch 18 §18.3.1 table row '70B dense FP16' and the paragraph immediately following the table
quoted_clause: 1 (140 GB weights across the 8-GPU pool, ~17.5 GB/GPU under TP; with KV, the full 640 GB pool is used) ... KV, not weights, is the binding term: as the FP16 row above notes, that tier's KV alone uses the full 640 GB pool, so this co-residency holds only while the resident tiers' combined KV fits.
observed: The chapter contradicts its own canonical KV budget. The book's canonical KV budget is 436 GB (640 GB pool - 140 GB FP16 weights - 64 GB overhead), and the same table's 4-bit row uses it explicitly ('canonical 436 GB KV budget reserved'). The FP16 row instead says the tier uses 'the full 640 GB pool', and the prose says 'that tier's KV alone uses the full 640 GB pool'. KV alone is 436 GB, not 640 GB. The two statements also cannot both describe the same pool: either the FP16 tier occupies the pool (no co-residency) or the pool holds 350 GB of weights plus ~290 GB of KV (co-residency with far less KV than the canonical 436 GB). The chapter never reconciles them, and the co-residency arithmetic is never carried through to the per-host concurrency C that Ch 17 depends on.
correction: Replace 'the full 640 GB pool is used' with the canonical 436 GB KV budget, and add the co-residency consequence: with 350 GB of resident weights the pool's KV falls to ~226 GB and C to ~9, which changes the fleet arithmetic in Ch 18 and Ch 17. If the intent is that the FP16 tier occupies the pool exclusively, remove the co-residency list and say so.
evidence: Canonical: 436 GB KV budget, C = 17 at 24.89 GB/request (Ch 17). Co-residency per §18.3.1: 640 - 350 (weights) - 64 (overhead) = 226 GB KV, C = floor(226/24.89) = 9, a 47% reduction in the FP16 tier's concurrency that the chapter does not mention. Without the unrouted 4-bit tier: 296 GB KV, C = 11.

page_hint: Ch 18 §18.3.2 'Basis note (reconciled with Ch16's TCO)'
quoted_clause: divides the full peak-provisioned fleet TCO (~$155,817/mo ≈ ~$156K/mo, 21 hosts at full utilization) by the token volume that fleet serves at the canonical workload — 6.24M requests/month × 9,500 tokens ≈ 5.93×10¹⁰ tokens/month — giving ~$155,817 ÷ 5.93×10¹⁰ ≈ **$2.63/1M**. That is close to — but not equal to — the $2.50/1M the table prints for the FP16 tier, and the closeness is a coincidence of this volume
observed: The monthly request volume used for the fleet-amortized rate is inconsistent with the canonical workload's stated average rate by a factor of about 4.2. The canonical workload is 10 rps average / 40 rps peak (Ch 17 §17.8 scenario; Ch 18 §18.3 scenario). 10 rps x 730 h x 3600 s/h = 26.28M requests/month, not 6.24M. 6.24M/month corresponds to ~2.37 rps average. The reconciliation note's central claim - that the fleet-amortized rate is 'close to' the FP16 nominal rate - depends entirely on this volume: at 26.28M requests/month the fleet-amortized rate is $155,817 / 2.4966e11 = $0.62/1M, i.e. 4x below the $2.50/1M table row, and the 'coincidence' narrative and the direction of the comparison both change.
correction: Reconcile the monthly volume with the canonical average rate, or state explicitly that 6.24M requests/month is a different scope (for example a single tenant or a measured subset) and label it as such. Then re-derive the fleet-amortized rate and rewrite the 'closeness is a coincidence' sentence against the corrected number.
evidence: 10 rps x 2,628,000 s = 26,280,000 requests/month. 6.24M / 2,628,000 s = 2.375 rps. 6.24M x 9,500 = 5.928e10 tokens (the printed token volume is arithmetically correct given 6.24M). $155,817 / 5.928e10 = $2.628/1M (correct given the stated inputs).
